summary: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organizations Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Conditions for Coverage, Final Rule (CMS ‑ 3409-F) Overview The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) published a final rule that will continue to strengthen federal oversight of Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs). This final rule expands on the December 2020 final rule that set the framework for performance metrics and created a tiered system to recertify or decertify OPOs based on their performance on both donation and transplant measures. It also clarifies designations to multiple donation service areas (DSAs), recertification processes, procedures for competition, appeals, information management, and other operational details. Background In 2019, President Trump issued Executive Order 13879 “Advancing American Kidney Health,” directing the Secretary to enhance the procurement and utilization of organs available through deceased donation and to establish more transparent, reliable, and enforceable objective metrics for evaluating an OPO’s performance. In response, CMS published the Organ Procurement Organization (OPO) Conditions for Coverage (CfCs) rule in December 2020. In January 2026, CMS published an additional proposed rule revising the OPO CfCs to clarify outstanding procedural questions and to enable OPOs to make more informed decisions to achieve high performance resulting in the successful procurement, distribution, and transplantation of more lifesaving organs (91 FR 4190). This final rule revises the CfCs for OPOs to clarify outstanding procedural questions for recertification and competition. This rule also revises definitions, clarifies the designation requirements for OPOs, clarifies when an OPO’s service area will be open for competition, and updates the appeals process. CMS remains committed to holding all OPOs accountable for their performance and will be moving to decertify tier 3 OPOs as indicated in the 2020 final rule. This final rule does not change the focus on improving donor and transplant volume, as assessed in the outcome measures, nor does it change the tier structure used for OPO recertification and decertification. The outcome measures focus on two rates — the donation rate and the transplantation rate. OPOs that have both DSAs ranking at or above the upper benchmark are placed in tier 1 and eligible for recertification for another four years. OPOs that have DSAs ranking in tier 2 are the next highest performers. Tier 2 OPO DSAs meet or exceed the lower benchmark on both measures but do not rate high enough to reach tier 1 on both measures. OPOs with DSAs that are in tier 2 are also eligible for recertification but must compete to retain their DSAs. Lastly, OPOs with tier 3 DSAs are the lowest performing OPOs with one or both measures below the lower benchmark. OPOs that only have tier 3 DSAs will be decertified and cannot compete for any other open DSA. The OPO final rule complements HHS’ recently released Kidney Care National Plan, a comprehensive strategy to restore competition and choice in dialysis care, reform the nation's organ transplant system, and prevent kidney failure before it begins. The plan identifies where federal action can improve kidney care across the entire spectrum of kidney disease and deliver greater choice and superior outcomes to Americans. Key Provisions for Strengthening Quality, Safety, and Oversight Unsound medical practices The rule defines “unsound medical practices” as failures by OPOs that create an imminent threat to patient health and safety or pose a risk to patients or the public. These practices include, but are not limited to, failures in governance; patient or potential donor evaluation and management; and procurement, allocation, and transport practices and procedures. This gives CMS a clear, enforceable basis for urgent decertification to protect patients and maintain public trust in the system. Adverse Events and Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) The rule removes the examples currently listed in the definition of “adverse event” and adds a revised list to the QAPI requirements. All OPOs must have QAPI programs that use data to monitor and improve their own performance. OPOs are specifically required to have policies for identifying, reporting, analyzing, and preventing adverse events that occur during the organ donation process. This change gives clear information so that all OPOs can act to prevent adverse events, investigate all adverse events, and take appropriate action to prevent future similar events. Pancreata Used for Islet Cell Research The rule clarifies that a donor whose pancreas is procured only for islet cell research counts as a donor for the donation rate measure. It removes pancreata used for islet cell research from the transplant rate measure, so islet cell research activity alone will no longer count as a transplant in the absence of a transplant. These refinements better incentivize both pancreata islet cell research and transplantation while more precisely measuring performance. Documentation of Research Organs This rule requires OPOs to maintain records on the disposition of organs recovered for bona fide research studies. This will foster OPO accountability in the responsible disposition of any organ sent for research, including pancreata that are used for islet cell research. Human Resources The rule requires an OPO’s medical director to hold a license in at least one of the states or territories within one of the OPO’s service areas, or as required by applicable law. This requirement addresses OPOs that operate in more than one DSA. Key Provisions for Incentivizing Fair and Equitable Competition to Increase Organ Donation and Transplantation Nonrenewal of Tier 2 OPO Agreements for Designation The rule clarifies that CMS will not renew an OPO’s agreement for designation to a DSA if the OPO is no longer designated to that DSA. This could occur if an OPO with a tier 2 DSA is unsuccessful in the competition process and fails to retain its DSA. In this situation, the OPO may compete for other DSAs or potentially be assigned a DSA by CMS in certain situations. Decertification The rule identifies circumstances in which CMS may involuntarily end an OPO’s agreement: The OPO no longer meets the requirements for certification, including process performance measures. All of the OPO’s DSAs fall into tier 3 in the final assessment period. An OPO is unsuccessful in competition to retain its tier 2 DSA, is not designated to any DSA, and does not have any performance data at the end of the following recertification cycle. In cases of urgent need, CMS may decertify an OPO immediately. This change clarifies that tier 2 status alone is not a basis for decertification, thereby allowing OPOs with tier 2 DSAs to be recertified. Appeals process The rule codifies a process for discretionary review by the CMS Administrator after a hearing officer issues a decision. Competition and DSA transitions The rule clarifies, without changing the regulation itself, how existing competition selection criteria apply under the tier system for recertification. In addition, it adds a new requirement for incumbent OPOs to cooperate with the successor OPO during a transition. It also requires the successor OPO to submit a transition plan with periodic progress reports to CMS. Together, these requirements support uninterrupted service to patients and donor families during a DSA transition. Requirements for certification The rule removes the requirement that an OPO must have been recertified under Medicare between Jan. 1, 2002, and Dec. 31, 2005. The OPO Final Rule complements the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) ongoing modernization of the national organ transplant system, including new governance, technology, and oversight improvements, to strengthen safety, transparency, and public trust. CMS’ OPO oversight and HRSA’s Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network modernization advance a common goal: safer procurement and more lifesaving transplants. CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organizations Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Conditions for Coverage, Final Rule (CMS 3409-F)

summary: Background: Chronic disease and comorbid mental health problems disproportionately affect rural and underserved populations. Digital self-management programs are potentially scalable, but evaluations often focus on narrow outcomes. Objective: This study examined 12-month longitudinal changes in psychological and multidomain outcomes among Pictou County Patient Empowerment Program participants and explored co-occurring changes and psychological moderators. Methods: This single-arm prospective interventional study enrolled 182 community-dwelling adults with ≥1 chronic condition in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, between October 2023 and August 2025 through community-based outreach. Median age was 60 (IQR 51‐68) years, 155 of 182 (85.2%) participants were women, and the median number of chronic conditions was 3 (IQR 1‐3). The initial 6-month digital intervention delivered brief daily modules targeting physical activity, nutrition, stress regulation, sleep, habit formation, and social connection, followed by a 6-month lower-intensity maintenance period during which monthly group videoconference sessions continued to be offered. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Primary outcomes were illness perceptions (Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire), perceived stress (10-item Perceived Stress Scale [PSS-10]), disease-related worry (10-item Questionnaire on Distress in Cancer Patients), life satisfaction (Satisfaction With Life Scale), and mental well-being (World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index [WHO-5]). Secondary outcomes assessed the physical, behavioral, and psychosocial domains. Generalized estimating equations estimated population-averaged longitudinal changes, adjusted for age, sex, relationship status, comorbidity burden, and baseline depression or anxiety medication use. Exploratory models examined co-occurring changes and moderation. Tests were 2-sided with =.05. Results: Across outcomes and follow-up assessments, completion ranged from 58.2% (95% CI 51.0%-65.2%; 106/182) to 65.4% (95% CI 58.2%‐71.9%; 119/182). At 12 months, illness perceptions decreased (β=−7.3, 95% CI −9.7 to −4.9), perceived stress decreased (β=−2.4, 95% CI −3.5 to −1.3), disease-related worry decreased (β=−6.3, 95% CI −7.8 to −4.7), life satisfaction increased (β=2.5, 95% CI 1.4‐3.5), and mental well-being increased (β=10.4, 95% CI 7.2‐13.5; all <.001). Secondary outcomes improved across fatigue, sleep, diet quality, sedentary behavior, spiritual well-being, mental health–related quality of life, weight, and BMI. Exploratory analyses showed that improvements in fatigue, sleep quality, and illness perceptions co-occurred with greater well-being and life satisfaction and lower perceived stress and disease-related worry at both follow-up assessment points. Clinically meaningful stress improvement (≥4-point PSS-10 reduction) was achieved by 36.4% (95% CI 27.3%-45.6%, 39/107) and 43.4% (95% CI 34.0%-52.8%, 46/106) participants at 6 and 12 months, respectively. At 12 months, 43.5% (95% CI 34.2%-52.9%, 47/108) participants reported clinically meaningful improvement in mental well-being (≥10-point WHO-5 increase). Conclusions: Participation in this low-bandwidth, home-based digital self-management program was associated with sustained psychological, physical, and behavioral improvements among rural adults with chronic conditions. These multidomain findings support randomized controlled evaluation of scalable digital self-management approaches as adjuncts to rural chronic disease care. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06064110; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06064110
title: Multidomain Outcomes of a Digital Self-Management Program in Rural Adults With Chronic Conditions: Single-Arm Prospective Interventional Study

summary: Plan Year 2027 Marketplace Plans and Prices Fact Sheet The Open Enrollment Period to choose Healthcare.gov coverage for 2027 begins on November 1, 2026, and runs through January 15, 2027. In the upcoming year, Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans. President Trump has delivered the largest decrease in Americans’ prescription drug prices in nearly 70 years; made historic investments to expand healthcare access in rural communities; and maximized price transparency. The Trump Administration continues to fight to lower insurance premiums and send money directly to the American people—not big insurance companies. Robust Access to Low-Cost Plans: More than 75% of Americans who purchase coverage through HealthCare.gov will continue to have access to premiums at or below $50 in 2027. The millions of Americans eligible for tax credits will have access to a plan with nearly 90% of the lowest-cost premium paid for by the federal government, compared to 85% in 2020—the last year not impacted by temporary COVID-19 policies. Building off the Historic Health Savings Account (HSA) Eligibility Expansion: Thanks to President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, every American purchasing healthcare through HealthCare.gov has access to HSA-eligible plans. HSAs allow American families to put more money back into their pockets by cutting taxes on healthcare while giving people, not insurance companies, greater control over their health spending. In 2027, eligible enrollees will have access to 35 different health plans on average that are HSA-eligible, a more than 1,000% increase over the status quo prior to President Trump’s historic Working Families Tax Cuts. Robust Choice: In 2027, families using HealthCare.gov will have access to a broad selection of plans to choose from. On average, Americans have access to 100 different plans and five to six different insurance companies. Low-Cost Catastrophic Plans: Catastrophic plans offer access to co-pay-free preventive care and protections for individuals with pre-existing conditions at lower costs. The average premium of the lowest-cost catastrophic plan is nearly 10% cheaper than the next lowest-cost plan at other coverage levels. The Trump Administration will continue to fight to lower drug prices and insurance premiums, hold big insurance companies accountable, and maximize price transparency. To learn more, visit whitehouse.gov/greathealthcare . CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Plan Year 2027 Marketplace Plans and Prices Fact Sheet

summary: Background: Recovery after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is typically assessed with infrequent clinic-based evaluations that may not reflect patients’ everyday mobility. Smartphone inertial sensors enable scalable, repeated gait measurement in real-world settings, but the extent to which prompted walking tests reflect daily life walking during recovery is not well defined. Objective: The objective of this study was to characterize week-by-week recovery trajectories after THA and TKA using high-frequency smartphone sensor data and quantify the difference between prompted in-app walking tests and passive daily life background walking. Methods: We analyzed longitudinal smartphone-based gait measurements from 735 patients (THA, n=350; TKA, n=385) who underwent unilateral surgery between July 2022 and October 2025. Nine spatiotemporal gait parameters were monitored over the first 15 postoperative weeks across 2 conditions: prompted “in-app” walks and passively captured “background” walks. Recovery trajectories were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier time-to-baseline analyses, linear mixed-effects models, and comparison of late-stage plateau levels (weeks 11‐15) using estimated marginal means of the models. Results: Across all parameters, THA patients returned to preoperative baseline levels faster than TKA patients, with mean trajectories generally approaching baseline by week 4 for THA versus weeks 6 to 8 for TKA. Linear mixed-effects models showed that surgical procedure type significantly influenced recovery trajectory for all parameters except single support of the unaffected leg. All gait parameters except stance asymmetry and single support of the unaffected leg exhibited persistent differences through the late-recovery plateau (weeks 11‐15). We also compared prompted “in-app” walks with passively captured background walking. Prompted and passive walking showed systematic divergence in both THA and TKA; prompted assessments generally indicated faster or more complete return to baseline than passive daily life walking. Finally, preoperative gait level was strongly associated with postoperative trajectories, with baseline-stratified analyses showing distinct patterns of recovery between groups. Conclusions: High-frequency smartphone gait assessment quantifies procedure-specific recovery dynamics and demonstrates that prompted tests and passive daily life measurements capture distinct, noninterchangeable functional signals. Parameters from prompted walks plateaued while those from passively captured walks were still changing; prompted testing alone therefore captures only one component of returning function, highlighting the additional information that passive, real-world gait monitoring can provide.
title: Real-World Functional Gait Recovery Trajectories After Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty via Smartphone Sensors: Observational Longitudinal Study

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models have enabled substantial advances across a wide range of healthcare applications. Since the entry into force of the Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the European Union intended to harmonize AI governance across all Member States. One of the Act’s distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we propose recommendations for the design of healthcare regulatory sandboxes. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 10²⁵ FLOPs threshold, to incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, to identify and document biases in healthcare datasets, to clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the GDPR, and to strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely, given the approaching deadline of 2 August 2026, by which all Member States must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox
title: Rethinking Health Care Regulatory Sandboxes Under the European Union AI Act

summary: Background: Prenatal depression and anxiety have emerged as pressing global public health challenges. In the digital era, excessive smartphone use may exert complex effects on maternal mental health. Prior research has predominantly focused on adolescents, whereas evidence among pregnant women, particularly regarding total weekly use and use during critical circadian windows, such as after waking and before bedtime, remains limited. Furthermore, the mediating role of sleep quality in these associations has yet to be systematically examined. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the associations of smartphone addiction and time-specific smartphone use with prenatal depression and anxiety, and to assess the mediating role of sleep quality in these associations. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study enrolled 537 pregnant women. Smartphone use characteristics, sleep quality, and prenatal depression and anxiety were assessed using the Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version (SAS-SV), objective total weekly smartphone use recorded by the device, and self-reported duration of smartphone use after waking and duration of bedtime smartphone use; the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), respectively. Binary logistic regression was used to estimate associations, restricted cubic spline (RCS) models were used to explore nonlinear patterns, and exploratory mediation analyses were used to examine whether sleep quality statistically accounted for part of the observed associations. Results: The prevalence of moderate-to-severe prenatal depression and anxiety was 8.8% (47/537) and 5.8% (31/537), respectively. After adjusting for covariates, smartphone addiction was associated with higher odds of depression (odds ratio [OR] 3.461, 95% CI 1.771‐7.100) and anxiety (OR 7.738, 95% CI 3.064‐23.172). Duration of smartphone use after waking ≥61 minutes and duration of bedtime smartphone use ≥91 minutes were also associated with higher odds of affective disorders. RCS analyses further revealed distinct nonlinear patterns across different exposure dimensions: duration of smartphone use after waking displayed U-shaped and J-shaped associations with depression and anxiety, respectively, while total weekly use displayed a U-shaped association with anxiety. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that the indirect pathways through sleep quality were statistically significant for the associations of bedtime smartphone use, weekly smartphone use, and smartphone addiction with prenatal depression, with mediation proportions of 44.89% (0.0065/0.0145), 31.30% (0.0056/0.0183), and 31.48% (0.0415/0.1315), respectively. The corresponding proportions in the anxiety models were 35.83% (0.0044/0.0123), 27.05% (0.0039/0.0144), and 22.73% (0.0271/0.1187). Conclusions: Smartphone addiction and excessive smartphone use after waking and before bedtime were associated with higher odds of prenatal depression and anxiety. Sleep quality may statistically account for part of these associations, but longitudinal studies are needed to establish temporal ordering and causal pathways.
title: The Mediating Role of Sleep Quality in Associations of Smartphone Addiction and Time-Specific Use With Prenatal Depression and Anxiety: Cross-Sectional Observational Study

summary: Background: While AI has existed for decades, the introduction of generative AI tools and subsequent advancements in their capability and public use resulted in a shift in public awareness and perceptions of AI. In response, the research community has grown increasingly interested in understanding public perceptions of AI use in various contexts, including health care. Public perceptions shape AI acceptance and consequently integration into health care. It is thus crucial to understand public trust in AI and perceptions of risk as we consider its implementation moving forward. Objective: This study aimed to (1) document the extent of what is known within the literature regarding public perceptions of AI applications in health; (2) interrogate existing definitions and theories of trust being used to guide investigations of public trust in AI; and (3) identify practice and policy considerations and support the design, deployment, and regulation of these technologies in a manner that is trustworthy. Methods: The Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines were used to review publications between 2022 and 2024 across 4 databases, resulting in the inclusion of 41 papers for review. Key findings were then charted and organized into tables to help answer the proposed research questions. Results: Public trust in AI in health care was shaped by discourse relating to AI performance and concerns related to depersonalization, loss of human connection, privacy, bias, and transparency. Trust was found to be higher when AI was supporting rather than replacing health care professionals and was influenced by emotional responses, anthropomorphism, demographic factors, and institutional trust. Furthermore, trust extended beyond algorithms to software interfaces, providers, developers, and governing institutions, highlighting the importance of governance and oversight. Conceptualizations of trust varied widely, and trust was defined through vulnerability, competence, benevolence, and integrity. Different theories identified suggested that trust operates across individual, social, institutional, and technological levels. Finally, trust was closely linked to risk and uncertainty, where perceived risk reduced acceptance, while AI literacy, transparency, and explainability mitigated concerns and fostered trust. Conclusions: Trust in AI is not uniform, and as such, efforts to build and measure trust must account for these nuances to effectively mitigate risk and support informed, ethical AI integration and deployment. On the basis of the findings of this review, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that provides a general understanding of public trust in AI within a health care context that may guide research and policy and practice considerations. Our findings highlight the importance of considering public trust when implementing AI in health care and may support AI communication strategies, policy development, and trustworthy AI development.
title: Trust, Risk, and Uncertainty Surrounding the Use of AI in Health Care: Scoping Review of Studies on Public Perception

summary:
Importance

Cesarean delivery is the most common surgery in the US and the most significant risk factor for postpartum infection. Although trial evidence demonstrated that adjunctive azithromycin use at the time of birth reduces postpartum infection in pregnant persons who undergo an unscheduled cesarean delivery, use of azithromycin outside that trial has not been reported.

Objective

To determine the adoption of trial evidence in clinical practice and describe postpartum infection trends among US pregnant persons undergoing unscheduled cesarean delivery.

Design, setting, and participants

Data from Epic Cosmos were used to conduct a difference-in-differences analysis including pregnant individuals who received prenatal care, labored, and gave birth to a liveborn singleton infant at 24 to 43 weeks' gestation from 2013 to 2024. Cesarean birth was considered the treatment group and vaginal birth was considered the control group. The analysis was conducted from July 2025 to June 2026.

Exposure

Relative to the publication of trial evidence in 2016, births that occurred from January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, were compared with births that occurred from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcomes were perioperative administration of azithromycin and postpartum infection within 6 weeks of delivery. Patient-level linear regression was used to obtain the difference-in-differences estimate.

Results

Of the 1 663 441 infant deliveries included in the analysis, there were 202 234 cesarean births and 1 461 207 vaginal births (mean age of pregnant individuals, 29.3 [SD, 5.7] years; median body mass index at time of delivery, 31.8 [IQR, 28.2-36.5]). From January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, azithromycin was administered during 2.2% of cesarean births (721/32 970) vs 0.01% of vaginal births (15/261 624) compared with 39.6% (67 094/169 264) vs 0.04% (421/1 199 583), respectively, from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024 (adjusted difference-in-differences estimate, 37.6 percentage points [95% CI, 33.1 to 42.2]). From January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, postpartum infection occurred after 9.2% of cesarean births (3048/32 970) vs 2.0% of vaginal births (5311/261 624) compared with 8.0% (13 555/169 264) vs 2.7% (32 581/1 199 583), respectively, from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024 (adjusted difference-in-differences estimate, -2.0 percentage points [95% CI, -2.6 to -1.4]).

Conclusions and relevance

After publication of the trial evidence in 2016, azithromycin use for pregnant persons undergoing unscheduled cesarean delivery increased and postpartum infection rates decreased in the US.
title: Adoption of Adjunctive Azithromycin for Unscheduled Cesarean Delivery and Postpartum Infections.

summary:
Background

Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) improves clinical outcomes. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) provides anatomical and physiological information before cardiac catheterization that may enable PCI planning. Data regarding the use of CCTA-guided PCI as compared with IVUS-guided PCI with respect to clinical outcomes are lacking.

Methods

In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial with blinded end-point adjudication, we randomly assigned patients with a clinical indication for revascularization, at least one epicardial lesion with a diameter stenosis of more than 70%, and a fractional flow reserve derived from CCTA of 0.80 or less in a 1:1 ratio to a CCTA-guided or IVUS-guided PCI strategy. The primary end point was target-vessel failure, defined as a composite of death from cardiac causes, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization, at 12 months. The noninferiority margin for the absolute risk difference was 4.5 percentage points, with a prespecified hierarchical testing strategy for superiority.

Results

A total of 1105 patients underwent randomization: 556 to the CCTA-guided PCI group and 549 to the IVUS-guided PCI group. The median age of the patients was 65 years, and 21.7% were women. At 12 months, target-vessel failure had occurred in 23 patients (4.1%) in the CCTA-guided PCI group and in 25 patients (4.6%) in the IVUS-guided PCI group (risk difference, -0.42 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -2.82 to 1.99; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.73 for superiority). A total of 6 patients in the CCTA-guided PCI group and 9 patients in the IVUS-guided PCI group had clinical procedural complications.

Conclusions

A CCTA-guided PCI strategy was noninferior to IVUS-guided PCI with respect to target-vessel failure at 12 months. (Funded by GE HealthCare and Heartflow; P4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05253677.).
title: Coronary CT Angiography versus Intravascular Ultrasound Guidance for PCI.

summary:
Importance

Statin nonadherence is a leading, addressable driver of preventable cardiovascular events. Although health systems routinely use outreach to promote preventive care, most strategies are static and lack evidence from randomized clinical trials.

Objective

To determine whether an adaptive, sequential digital outreach strategy improves short-term statin refill vs usual communication among adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or high ASCVD risk and recent nonadherence within a rapidly implemented, health system-embedded randomized clinical trial.

Design, setting, and participants

Pragmatic, health system-embedded, prospective randomized open blinded end point (PROBE) clinical trial using a 2-stage sequential, multiple assignment, randomized trial (SMART) design. The trial was conducted via Kaiser Permanente Northern California, an integrated health care delivery system serving more than 4.6 million members. Eligible participants were adults 18 years or older with established ASCVD or high ASCVD risk, recent statin nonadherence, and eligibility for all study communication modalities.

Interventions

Participants were randomized 1:1:1:1 to receive secure portal messaging, SMS/text messaging, nonsecure email, or usual communication. Initial nonresponders within 14 days underwent prespecified second-stage randomization to repeat the same outreach, switch communication modality, or receive usual communication.

Main outcomes and measures

Rates of 14-day statin refill following each randomization, with 28-day follow-up.

Results

Among 20 604 participants (mean [SD] age, 54.8 [9.0] years; 40.9% female; 27.8% Asian, 10.9% Black, 33.6% Hispanic; 15.3% with established ASCVD), initial digital outreach increased 14-day statin refill vs usual communication (14.4% vs 12.0%; adjusted risk difference, 2.3 percentage points [95% CI, 1.3-3.4]; adjusted risk ratio, 1.20 [95% CI, 1.10-1.30]). Among initial nonresponders, second-stage outreach further increased refill (13.0% vs 10.4%; adjusted risk difference, 2.5 percentage points [95% CI, 1.3-3.7]; adjusted risk ratio, 1.25 [95% CI, 1.11-1.39]). Switching communication modalities did not improve refill vs repeating the same modality (13.2% vs 12.5%; adjusted risk ratio, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.94-1.17]). Cumulative statin refill through 28 days was higher in those receiving any digital outreach vs usual communication (24.9% vs 21.2%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.13-1.30]). Results were consistent across prespecified subgroups.

Conclusions and relevance

Among adults with a statin indication and recent statin nonadherence, adaptive outreach improved short-term refill vs usual communication. A second outreach produced additional gains among initial nonresponders, although switching communication modalities provided no additional benefit. These findings support adaptive, sequential health system outreach strategies to improve cardiovascular prevention when integrated into population health programs.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07522645.
title: Digital Outreach to Improve Statin Refills in Patients With Low Statin Adherence: The ADHERE-ASCVD Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Whether intravenous tenecteplase before endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) improves outcomes in patients with basilar artery occlusion presenting 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset remains uncertain.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT vs EVT alone in patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, open-label, blinded end point, randomized clinical trial was conducted at 40 stroke centers in China. Between March 16, 2023, and February 4, 2025, a total of 330 patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score ≥10) presenting within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset to EVT-capable centers were enrolled. Final follow-up was completed on May 4, 2025.

Interventions

Patients were randomized 1:1 via a centralized web server using a minimization method to receive either intravenous tenecteplase (bolus injection, 0.25 mg/kg; maximum, 25 mg) followed by EVT (n = 166) or EVT alone (n = 164).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was functional independence (modified Rankin Scale score, 0-2) at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 90-day mortality.

Results

Among 332 patients randomized, 2 withdrew consent. Of the remaining 330 patients (mean [SD] age, 66 [11] years; 241 males [73%]; 89 females [27%]), 329 completed 90-day follow-up. Of whom, 50 of 165 (30%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 50 of 164 (30%) in the EVT alone group achieved functional independence (adjusted rate ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.67 to 1.25]; risk difference, -0.18% [95% CI, -10.13% to 9.76%]). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 8 patients (5%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 6 (4%) in the EVT alone group. Mortality at 90 days was similar between the groups (66 [40%] vs 70 [43%], respectively).

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted directly to EVT-capable centers who presented 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset, the addition of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT did not result in improved functional outcomes compared with EVT alone.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05701956.
title: Tenecteplase Before Thrombectomy at 4.5 to 24 Hours for Basilar Artery Occlusion: The ATTENTION LATE Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Following a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) procedure, antithrombotic therapy is administered to safely allow time for device endothelialization. However, the optimal postimplant antithrombotic regimen is unknown.

Objective

To determine if either reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or aspirin alone are noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for the composite clinical end point of death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding through 6 months post LAAC.

Design, setting, and participants

This open-label, 3-group, multicenter clinical trial randomized 1857 patients between October 2024 and December 2025 at 87 US investigational sites, with the final 6-month follow-up in July 2026. Enrolled patients had nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, underwent successful LAAC, and were eligible for all 3 regimens.

Interventions

Patients were randomly allocated 1:1:1 to DAPT for 6 months followed by aspirin (n = 624), a reduced-dose NOAC for 3 months followed by aspirin (n = 620), or aspirin alone for 12 months (n = 613).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was the 6-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding. Noninferiority was tested in the primary analysis population with a 1-sided Farrington-Manning test (α = .025). Bleeding and 45-day device-related thrombus rates were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment.

Results

The cohort had a mean age of 76 (SD, 8) years, 42.9% were female, the mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2 (SD, 1.3), and 68.0% had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) with DAPT vs 31 (5.1%) with a reduced-dose NOAC (risk ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.48-1.18]; risk difference, -1.7 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, 1.2) and 20 (3.3%) with aspirin alone (risk ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29-0.82]; risk difference, -3.5 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, -0.8). Both monotherapy strategies met noninferiority criteria (P < .001 for noninferiority for both). Major bleeding was 4.5% with DAPT, 2.7% with reduced-dose NOACs, and 1.7% with aspirin alone; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 8.7%, 4.8%, and 3.8%, respectively. Device-related thrombus was observed in 3.4%, 0.9%, and 2.7%, respectively.

Conclusions and relevance

Both reduced-dose NOACs and aspirin alone were noninferior to DAPT for 6-month outcomes after uncomplicated LAAC.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06521463.
title: Antithrombotic Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: The SIMPLAAFY Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary: Background: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classifies chronic kidney disease (CKD) using categories based on both glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria. Structured measures remain essential but may not capture contextual clinical concerns documented in narrative records. Objective: This study examined whether text-derived clinical-status language features in clinician notes were associated with deterioration in renal function in independent Greek- and English-language clinical cohorts. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed a Greek general-nephrology cohort (314 patients; 10,306 estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] measurements) and an independent English-language Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) replication cohort. The Greek primary analysis used a linear mixed effects model over a follow-up period of up to 1797 days. The MIMIC-IV primary analysis used a 90-day, patient-level fixed-horizon competing-outcome model (N=87,533). Separate analyses of Greek and MIMIC-IV data evaluated discrimination, calibration, and sensitivity to alternative feature specifications. Results: In the Greek cohort, a 1-SD higher negativity was associated with lower eGFR (=−3.273 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% CI −5.049 to −1.498; <.001) and a more negative time trajectory (time-by-score =−1.324, 95% CI −2.553 to −0.096; =.035). In MIMIC-IV, a 1-SD higher negative-vs-reassuring polarity contrast was associated with renal deterioration (relative risk ratio [RRR]=1.090, 95% CI 1.070‐1.110; <.001). Within eGFR G categories, polarity-score areas under the curve (AUCs) were 0.506 to 0.552 using discharge eGFR and 0.518 to 0.534 using the worst observed eGFR. Discrimination for renal deterioration remained modest (one-vs-rest AUC=0.6134, 95% CI 0.6092‐0.6175), and adding both natural language processing (NLP) features to the clinical model increased AUC by only 0.0018 (95% CI 0.0010‐0.0025). Conclusions: Independently constructed clinical-language measures were associated with renal function deterioration across two languages and health care settings. The findings support cross-language replication of an association signal, not formal external validation, measurement equivalence, or clinically useful stand-alone prediction.
title: Context-Dependent Clinical Narrative Signals of Renal Function Deterioration in Cross-Language Settings: Retrospective Multicohort Study

summary: Background: Continuous patient monitoring generates vast volumes of high-frequency monitoring data, such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and invasive blood pressure tracings, that are often persisted in heterogeneous, noninteroperable formats, limiting integration with electronic health records and secondary use. Although Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) supports general health data exchange, native support for high-frequency medical monitoring data, including associated metadata and data quality metrics, remains limited. Objective: This study aims to develop a modality-agnostic FHIR package implementing a pattern to enable scalable, semantically precise representation of high-frequency medical monitoring data, decoupling structured clinical metadata from raw signal storage. Methods: This study provides the FHIR package Time Series Integration and Data in Endpoints (TIDE), a collection of FHIR Release 4 artifacts for interoperable exchange and the standardization of high-frequency monitoring clinical data, using electroencephalography as the primary use case while remaining applicable to generic medical monitoring data. The core TIDE profile separates technical metadata and analytical summaries stored directly in FHIR from high-volume raw data referenced via resources. Quantitative results are standardized with pattern slicing, including sampling frequency, statistical summaries, and data quality metrics. Semantic interoperability was achieved through a hybrid terminology binding, using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms, Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes for modalities, and custom for technical metadata, waveform modalities, channel identifiers, and connection types not covered by standard terminologies. All profiles were authored in FHIR Shorthand and compiled with SUSHI to produce a validated Implementation Guide conformant with the FHIR Release 4 core specification. Results: The resulting framework provides a modality-agnostic structure for high-frequency monitoring data, comprising 7 primary FHIR artifacts that define 16 distinct component slices for metadata and signal analysis results. resources reference associated and instances, encapsulate acquisition parameters, and link to full-time-series repositories. Controlled vocabularies ensure unambiguous exchange, thereby enabling downstream use in research and decision support. The architecture decouples the metadata layer from the storage layer via a standardized extension, enabling efficient querying of signals without retrieving large amounts of raw high-frequency monitoring data. Conclusions: TIDE provides a reusable, standards-compliant framework for integrating continuous high-frequency monitoring data into FHIR-based ecosystems. By separating semantically rich, queryable metadata from raw signal storage, TIDE enables longitudinal patient monitoring and automated signal quality-based triage without requiring modification of existing signal storage infrastructure.
title: Exchange of High-Frequency Medical Monitoring Data Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources for Interoperable Integration Into Clinical Practice and Research: Methodological Development Study

summary: Background: The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application. Objective: This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective. Methods: A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression. Results: The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI, ²=0.759), 67% in perceived usefulness (PU, ²=0.670), and 54% in perceived risk (PR, ²=0.540). PU showed the strongest positive association with BI (=.670, <.001, ²=0.457), whereas PR showed a small negative association (=−.149, =.04, ²=0.034). Transparency was positively associated with PU (=.220, =.001) and perceived ease of use (PEOU; =.454, <.001) and negatively associated with PR (=−.594, <.001). Perceived need (PN) showed a strong positive association with PU (=.567, <.001) but no significant direct association with BI (=.071, =.35). Eight of 20 hypotheses were supported. Only 23.5% (n=35) of participants reported actual ePA use. BI showed a positive but imprecise and nonsignificant association with self-reported actual use (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.89-2.11, =.15). Measurement quality was mixed: reflective constructs generally showed satisfactory reliability and convergent validity; however, discriminant validity between PU and BI was poor (heterotrait-monotrait ratio of correlations [HTMT]=0.981). Conclusions: PU showed the strongest association with behavioral intention in the ePA case evaluation, while transparency and PN were mainly associated with behavioral intention through indirect pathways. The findings suggest potential value in extending traditional acceptance models with governance-related constructs relevant to HDSs. However, the severe overlap between PU and behavioral intention, low actual ePA uptake, and the young, highly educated convenience sample limit confidence in the magnitude and distinctiveness of the observed effects. HDS-TAM should therefore be regarded as a promising but preliminary framework requiring further refinement and validation.
title: Health Dataspace Technology Acceptance Model (HDS-TAM): Development and Case Evaluation Study of Patient Acceptance of Germany’s Electronic Patient Record

summary: Background: Machine learning has been extensively applied in medical prediction; however, existing machine-assisted pharmacotherapy review systems predominantly rely on structured, codifiable data while neglecting unstructured natural language clinical narratives, thereby allowing latent medication risks to remain undetected. Objective: To address the limitations of structured data–based review, this study proposes and validates a machine learning framework grounded in text classification for the automated identification of “prophylactic” vs “nonprophylactic” medication indications within clinical narratives. As a result, it aims to assist in the automated detection of prophylactic indication mentions for stress-related mucosal disease in clinical narratives as a preliminary step toward comprehensive medication-use review. Methods: A total of 3695 progress notes were independently annotated by 2 clinical pharmacists to construct a binary dataset for classifying prophylactic medication indication for stress-related mucosal disease, yielding an interannotator agreement κ of 0.8934. Comparative experiments were conducted using traditional machine learning models, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, CatBoost, and LightGBM, alongside TextCNN and a Chinese pretrained BERT model. The dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets on a patient-wise basis, and model evaluation was conducted on the independent test set. SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis was used to achieve model interpretability and elucidate decision-making processes, ultimately enabling automated indication detection of prophylactic proton pump inhibitor administration. Results: All models and strategies demonstrated efficacy in medical text classification tasks. In a single-center cohort of 66 patients (3695 notes, 11.0% positive), the CatBoost model with balanced class weights achieved a note-level -score of 0.727 (precision=0.693; recall=0.765) and a patient-level -score of 0.889 (precision=0.800; recall=1.000) on the independent test set. At the note level, CatBoost achieved a higher -score than TextCNN (-score=0.718) and BERT (-score=0.628). Conclusions: In summary, the text classifier constructed through machine learning and natural language processing effectively extracts prophylactic medication indications for stress-related mucosal disease from unstructured progress notes. Combined with patient-level data partitioning, standardized annotation protocols, and an ethics-compliant framework, this approach provides an interpretable preliminary screening tool for identifying potential prophylactic indications to support subsequent pharmacist adjudication. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2600126317; https://tinyurl.com/yjzjd443
title: Machine Learning–Based Detection of Prophylactic Indication Mentions for Stress-Related Mucosal Disease in Chinese Clinical Progress Notes: Text Classification Study

summary: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk. RetiME is a deep learning-based biomarker that maps retinal features to individual mortality risks and can reconstruct personalized lifespan trajectories associated with observed mortality outcomes with distinct disease-related mortality patterns.
title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories

summary:
Background

For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown.

Methods

We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population.

Results

A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement.

Conclusions

Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).
title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features.

summary: Background: Despite growing recognition that AI-driven systems offer transformative benefits for diagnostic imaging, insufficient evidence exists regarding how medical imaging workforces adapt to AI technology to support workforce sustainability. Objective: The aim of this study is to systematically review the existing literature on perceptions and attitudes toward AI adoption in medical imaging, postadoption adaptation behaviors within the workforce, and the implications of these processes for workforce sustainability. Methods: Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, a systematic search was carried out across 7 databases. Thematic analysis was used to systematically identify, analyze, and interpret patterns across the literature, providing a comprehensive understanding of workforce perceptions and adaptation behaviors. Results: A total of 69 peer-reviewed articles were included for thematic synthesis. The findings produced 6 critical factors that were identified as themes associated with AI adoption: perceived benefits, trust, readiness to change, autonomy and control, perceived threat to professional identity, and attitudes and intentions toward AI adoption and use. Four key facets of effective cognitive and behavioral adaptation were identified: training and skills development, task performance during AI-assisted practice, reduction of mental health burden and work strain, and policy compliance. The influence of work engagement and job satisfaction on workforce sustainability was also conceptualized. The findings were integrated into a framework describing the radiology workforce perspectives on AI adoption, adaptation behaviors, and workforce sustainability. Conclusions: The findings have potential implications for policy, particularly in strengthening AI-equipped medical imaging systems, fostering trust in AI-driven technologies, and supporting workforce training and upskilling, while considering professional autonomy and role identity. The review highlights a research gap, emphasizing the need for further investigation into postadoption adaptation processes and informing policy development that links AI integration with long-term workforce sustainability in medical imaging.
title: AI Adoption, Adaptation, and Workforce Sustainability in Medical Imaging: Systematic Review and Conceptual Framework

summary: Physicians, artificial intelligence developers and healthcare organizations that deploy clinical AI tools all bear distinct responsibilities for ensuring the tools do not cause patient harm, the American Medical Association said in an issue brief released last week. While physicians remain responsible for exercising their clinical judgment, developers are accountable for designing safe AI tools, the physician advocacy group said. At the same time, deployers are responsible for selecting the right tool for clinical scenarios, providing physicians' training and monitoring the AI's performance. Currently, physicians are being asked to become a safety net to protect against clinical AI failures that could harm patients, but that means they may be held accountable for risks that they cannot control and, "in some cases, may not even be able to identify," Jennifer Goldsack, head of the AMA Center on Digital Health and AI, said in an interview.
title: AI vendors, health systems join physicians in liability for clinical AI: AMA

summary: Background: Early childhood caries (ECC) is a prevalent yet preventable disease that significantly impacts young children’s health and quality of life. The World Health Organization’s highlights the potential of mobile health programs to enhance engagement and support sustained oral health behavior change. Objective: The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of the SmilesUp 12-week SMS text messaging–based education and support program to improve parents’ management of their children’s oral health behaviors compared to standard clinical care. Methods: We conducted a multisite, assessor-blinded, parallel-design randomized controlled trial among parents of children aged 0 to 6 years who had an ECC diagnosis and attended 1 of 6 public dental clinics in metropolitan, regional, and rural New South Wales, Australia. Participants were randomly assigned to either an intervention group receiving the fully automated 12-week SmilesUp program (3 SMS text messages weekly) or a control group. Both groups continued to receive usual standard dental clinical treatment. The primary behavioral outcome was parent-reported twice-daily toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste. Secondary outcomes included adherence to oral health–promoting bedtime routines and child consumption of sugar-sweetened foods and beverages. Oral health self-efficacy was measured using 6 behavioral theory–mapped items across oral hygiene, diet, and bedtime routines. Results: A total of 154 participants were enrolled and randomized (n=78, 50.6% in the control group; n=76, 49.4% in the intervention group) across 6 sites, with 80.5% (124/154) completing the follow-up assessment. High program adherence was observed, with 96.1% (73/76) of intervention participants completing the program. At 12 weeks, a greater proportion of SmilesUp participants reported brushing their children’s teeth twice daily (45/61, 73.8% vs 42/63, 66.7%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.45, 95% CI 0.95-6.74; =.07), though this difference was not statistically significant. Significant improvements were observed in adherence to bedtime routines (54/61, 88.5% vs 45/63, 71.4%; aOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.15-10.18; =.03) as well as oral health knowledge on toothbrushing (46/50, 92.0% vs 41/52, 78.8%; aOR 5.47, 95% CI 1.48-25.19; =.02). No statistically significant differences were found in sugar-sweetened food (10/61, 16.4% vs 4/63, 6.3%; aOR 3.72, 95% CI 1.02-17.14; =.06) or beverage (25/61, 41.0% vs. 27/63, 42.9%; aOR 1.08, 95% CI 0.49-2.30; =.85) consumption. Conclusions: These findings suggest that co-designed SMS text messaging–based programs show promise and may represent a feasible strategy for oral health behavior change. However, larger-scale and longer-term studies are needed to confirm sustained effectiveness using clinical outcomes. Future research should also explore ways mobile health can be scaled and cost-effectively embedded into comprehensive, interdisciplinary primary models of care. Trial Registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12623000325606; https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12623000325606 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.1371/journal.pone.0310561
title: Co-Designed Text Messaging Intervention for Parents of Children With Early Childhood Caries: Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Repurposing approved drugs offers a time- and cost-effective alternative to traditional drug development. However, in silico prediction of repurposing candidates is challenging and requires the effective collaboration of specialists in various fields, including pharmacology, medicine, biology, and bioinformatics. Fragmented, specialized algorithms and tools often address only narrow aspects of the overall problem. Heterogeneous, unstructured data landscapes require the expertise of specialized users. Hence, diverse data sources might not integrate smoothly across workflows. Objective: We aimed to develop an integrated, natural language–driven system that enables domain experts to conduct complex network-based drug repurposing analyses by integrating heterogeneous biomedical data sources and specialized bioinformatics methods within a unified workflow. Methods: With ChatDRex, we present a conversation-based, multi-agent system that facilitates the execution of complex bioinformatic analyses aiming for network-based drug repurposing prediction. It builds on the integrated systems medicine knowledge graph NeDRexDB. ChatDRex provides natural language access to its extensive biomedical knowledge base. It integrates bioinformatics agents for network analysis, literature mining, and drug repurposing. These are complemented by agents that evaluate functional coherence for in silico validation. Its flexible multi-agent design assigns specific tasks to specialized agents, including query routing, data retrieval, algorithm execution, and result visualization. A dedicated reasoning module keeps the user in the loop and allows for hallucination detection. Results: ChatDRex operationalizes complex network-based drug repurposing workflows through conversational interaction, integrating biomedical knowledge access with algorithm execution and validation-oriented assessments. Its modular multi-agent architecture enables scalable task specialization across retrieval, analysis, validation, and visualization, while the reasoning module provides transparency and safeguards against unreliable outputs. Conclusions: By enabling researchers with limited computational expertise to control complex analyses with natural language, ChatDRex could democratize access to bioinformatics as an important resource for drug repurposing. It could enable clinical experts to generate hypotheses and explore drug repurposing opportunities, ultimately accelerating the discovery of novel therapies and advancing personalized medicine and translational research.
title: Conversational Multi-Agentic Network-Driven Disease Module Identification and Drug Repurposing Prediction With ChatDRex: Platform Development Study

summary:
Background

Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States.

Objective

To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups.

Design

Cohort study using the target trial framework.

Setting

Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial.

Patients

Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months.

Intervention

Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone.

Measurements

The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade.

Results

Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ.

Limitation

Possible residual confounding.

Conclusion

Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months.

Primary funding source

Research Council of Norway.
title: Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis : A Target Trial Emulation.

summary: Background: Digital decision-support tools such as triage systems and symptom checkers support millions of health-related decisions each year. Their quality and safety are commonly evaluated using textual patient cases, known as case vignettes. However, expert-written vignette sets cover only a limited spectrum of real-world patient presentations and lack population weights, which would allow extrapolating evaluation results to the underlying patient population. Objective: This study aimed to develop a data-driven framework for automatically generating a human-manageable set of case vignettes from nationwide triage data that capture broad presentation diversity and link each vignette to a quantitative weight reflecting the number of underlying patient assessments. Methods: From 3.2 million triage assessments conducted over 1 year using structured triage software in the German medical on-call service (telephone triage and online self-triage) and at joint contact points of the outpatient emergency care service and hospital emergency departments, we randomly sampled 50,000 cases. Triage questionnaires were converted into semantic embeddings using a German Sentence Transformer model and grouped by agglomerative clustering. For clusters containing sufficient assessments, we generated one representative assessment using a 2-phase simulated annealing optimization that minimized the distance from the cluster centroid while maximizing the number of answered triage questions. Each representative assessment was assigned the size of its source cluster as its sample-based weight. A similarity-based sensitivity analysis assessed whether these weights were preserved in the full 1-year population. Finally, question-answer pairs of the representative assessments were converted into textual case vignettes using controlled prompting of a large language model. Results: The cluster analysis yielded 514 included clusters covering 96.8% of the sampled 50,000 assessments. The generated representatives showed strong agreement with the majority treatment urgency recommendation of their source cluster (Spearman ρ=0.78; <.001) and contained, on average, 4.3 more answered triage questions than the original assessments within their clusters. When weighted by cluster size, the representatives approximated the sample distributions of treatment urgency, demographics, and symptoms, although some systematic deviations remained, most notably an overrepresentation of female cases (13.5%), patients aged 14‐49 (8.0%) years, and the urgency category “As soon as possible” (6.6%). Of 121 recorded symptoms, 101 (83.5%) were covered by the representatives; the rest each occurred in <0.5% of the sample. Cluster-based vignette weights were strongly correlated with similarity-based population weights (Spearman ρ=0.77; <.001), and 90.1% of assessments in the full 1-year population matched at least one vignette. Conclusions: We present a data-driven framework for deriving a manageable set of population-weighted case vignettes from nationwide triage data. The resulting vignettes captured broad presentation diversity, approximated key sample characteristics, and provided an explicit quantitative link to the number of underlying assessments. After medical expert review and refinement, the vignettes may support more population-aware evaluation and quality assurance of digital decision-support tools.
title: Generating Population-Linked Case Vignettes From Nationwide Triage Data: Framework Development and Validation Study

summary: Background: AI scribing tools to assist health care providers by generating clinical notes are rapidly spreading across health care settings. Although these tools may reduce documentation burden, successful implementation depends on the contextual factors influencing their integration into clinical practice. Implementation evaluations are needed to inform practice integration, guide future adoption, and enhance effective use of this novel technology. Objective: This study aims to explore contextual factors influencing the implementation of an AI scribe for physicians in the ambulatory setting. Methods: This study was a single-site qualitative implementation evaluation at a metropolitan university health system where the AI scribe was available across primary and specialty care clinics. The Practical, Robust Implementation and Sustainability Model (PRISM) and the Sociotechnical Systems framework guided the evaluation. Using maximum variation sampling, we recruited attending physicians with varied levels of AI scribe use. Semistructured interviews were conducted with attending physicians working in the ambulatory setting. Data collection and analysis occurred iteratively until thematic saturation was achieved. Interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis with a constant comparative method, incorporating both deductive and inductive coding. Resulting subthemes were mapped onto corresponding domains of the PRISM and Sociotechnical Systems frameworks. Results: A total of 25 physicians were interviewed, including 7 who had never used the AI scribe, 9 who used it minimally, and 9 who used it frequently. Participants represented a broad range of specialties. A total of 5 themes and 15 subthemes emerged. First, workflow integration influenced adoption. Limitations in customization were a barrier to adoption, while flexibility among users was critical to fit. Second, ease of tool usability facilitated initial adoption, whereby users tried the tool without paying close attention to training materials. However, this lack of training engagement hindered widespread sustained use due to limited knowledge of advanced functionalities. Third, attending physicians balanced trust and confidence in AI-generated documentation with mistrust and professional accountability. Many described a “trust but verify” approach. Also, some concerns about others’ inadequate review of AI-generated content weakened physician-physician trust. Fourth, attending physicians viewed the ubiquitous presence of AI scribing as inevitable, driven by organizational priorities related to productivity, cost, and burnout. Interviewees disagreed about the appropriate use of AI scribes by trainees. Finally, identical mechanisms were viewed as both benefits and drawbacks. Increased efficiency from AI documentation was perceived by some as reducing burden and cognitive load, but perceived by others as potentially intensifying workload expectations. Similarly, some thought AI scribes facilitated more patient-centered communication, while others thought it had the opposite impact. Conclusions: Implementation of AI scribes in ambulatory care is shaped by complex sociotechnical and contextual factors. Adoption is influenced by workflow alignment, trust, and preexisting beliefs about the tool’s benefits and drawbacks, illustrating how clinical context affects AI scribe implementation.
title: Implementation Evaluation of an AI Scribing Tool in the Ambulatory Setting: Single-Site Qualitative Implementation Evaluation Study

summary: Biomedical and health informatics (BMHI) has traditionally focused on human-centric clinical data to support individual patient care and health systems. However, contemporary health challenges driven by climate change, biodiversity loss, and ecological degradation demand an expanded paradigm that addresses interdependencies among human, animal, and environmental health. This editorial introduces a new JMIR Medical Informatics section on “Planetary Health Informatics” (PHI), an essential evolution extending informatics praxis beyond human healthcare toward Earth’s interconnected systems. JMIR Medical Informatics is launching a call for papers for a new section dedicated to advancing PHI theory, methods, and applications for a sustainable future shaped by human impact on Earth. We invite authors to submit work that explores how PHI integrates species, ecosystem, and geophysical data to address critical global challenges, including metagenomic disease surveillance, climate-related hazard forecasting, environmental pollution monitoring, and health infrastructure decarbonization. By synthesizing broader ecological frameworks, we present a roadmap for transforming fragmented data streams into planetary-scale intelligence.
title: Informatics for the Planet: Integrating Species, Ecosystems, and Geophysical Data to Manage the Health of Earth Systems

summary: Vagus nerve stimulation has shown promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in progressive neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. However, its invasive nature introduces procedural and device-related risks. Here we introduce a magnetoelectric particulate system for oral delivery and non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation through the gut. The system comprises a magneto-responsive nickel ferrite core and a piezoelectric barium titanate shell, conjugated with capsaicin to specifically target TRPV1 receptors, ensuring effective adherence to the stomach lining after oral administration. Upon magnetic field stimulation, the particles generate electrical pulses that activate vagal afferent fibres, engaging the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem via the gut−brain axis. This activation enhances norepinephrine production in the locus coeruleus and dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra. Vagal efferent activation triggers the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, mitigating both neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation. This non-invasive approach demonstrates potential for alleviating motor symptoms and non-motor anxiety in Parkinson’s disease, offering valuable insights into its mechanisms and clinical applications. Orally delivered magnetoelectric particles activate vagal afferent fibres in the gut−brain axis and influence neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease.
title: Non-invasive oral magnetoelectric vagus nerve neuromodulation for Parkinson’s disease therapy

summary: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) holds considerable promise across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, offering a practical path to patient-level diagnostic support. Foundation models further extend this potential by learning generalizable representations from large-scale unlabeled data, alleviating the burden of extensive manual annotation. However, existing ophthalmic foundation models largely rely on single-modality or modality-specific encoders, failing to capture patient-level cross-modal correspondence in real-world multimodal clinical workflows. To address these gaps, we propose RETBind, a patient-level multimodal foundation model with a unified encoder that explicitly learns cross-modal correspondence from paired clinical imaging using patient-level paired optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultra-widefield (UWF) fundus imaging. This patient-level paired pretraining strategy enables the model to learn unified cross-modal representations of complementary information, improv-ing performance and robustness beyond single-modality approaches. Across nine benchmark datasets spanning ocular disease classification and segmentation tasks, RETBind achieved consistent improvements, particularly enhancing AUPR in clinically relevant imbalanced settings. Exploratory analyses further examined the potential of RETBind for systemic disease prediction from retinal imaging, collectively highlighting its ability to learn unified cross-modal representations within a single shared encoder, enabling direct interaction between modalities and supporting transfer across diverse retinal imaging tasks.
title: RETBind: a patient-level multimodal foundation model for unified cross-modal retinal representation learning
