summary: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) complicated by unstable angina (UA) represents a major challenge in chronic disease management with high risk of recurrent heart failure hospitalization (HFH), and despite the availability of multicenter real-world data, AI-driven tools for multi-horizon risk assessment remain limited. This multicenter retrospective cohort enrolled 4367 patients with UA and HFpEF, and an ensemble feature selection pipeline integrating LASSO, SVM-RFE and Boruta identified robust predictors, followed by training of twelve machine learning algorithms to estimate HFH risk at 12-, 24- and 36-month horizons with external validation. The optimal time-specific models (ET, GBDT and LightGBM) achieved strong discrimination in the training cohort with AUCs of 0.818, 0.834 and 0.863, and maintained performance in external validation with AUCs of 0.839, 0.836 and 0.851, respectively, while SHAP analysis highlighted diabetes mellitus, TyG-BMI and NT-proBNP as the most influential predictors. We developed and externally validated a multi-time-point machine learning framework for HFH risk stratification in UA and HFpEF, which showed acceptable calibration and potential clinical utility on decision-curve analysis. Further prospective and real-world validation across diverse populations and healthcare systems is needed to confirm clinical effectiveness and support translation into routine practice.
title: AI-driven multi-horizon risk stratification for heart failure hospitalization in UA with HFpEF: a Chinese multi-center cohort study

summary: Background: The American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification system fundamentally shapes perioperative care delivery but suffers from poor interrater reliability (0.4‐0.6). Machine learning (ML) models and large language models (LLMs) offer complementary remedies: ML processes structured data consistently but cannot interpret the nuance of clinical narratives, while LLMs parse narrative text and generate explanations but adhere inconsistently to diagnostic criteria. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate a parallel ML-LLM ensemble that combines the complementary strengths of both approaches for automated ASA-PS classification. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 3000 adult surgical encounters from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences (UAMS) between August 2024 and May 2025. Cases were randomly allocated to training (n=2000), validation (N=500), and held-out test sets (N=500). The validation set was used exclusively for architecture comparison and hyperparameter tuning, and the held-out test set was reserved for final model performance validation. We developed multiple architectures, including traditional ML models (Extreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost], Light Gradient Boosting Machine [LightGBM], ExtraTrees), an LLM-only baseline (Generative Pretrained Transformer-4o [GPT-4o]), and hybrid approaches. The parallel ensemble processed structured data through XGBoost and unstructured clinical notes through GPT-4o independently, with outputs combined via weighted averaging. Model performance was evaluated using macro--score, exact match accuracy, and ±1-class accuracy. Results: A theoretical performance ceiling of macro--score=0.59 was determined through evaluation by an expert panel of 2 board-certified anesthesiologists (AF and GF) who independently rated 50 patient charts for ASA-PS scores. On the true held-out test set (N=500), the parallel ensemble (=0.30) achieved a macro--score of 0.530 (95% CI 0.350‐0.600), exact match accuracy of 0.630 (95% CI 0.580‐0.670), and ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968‐0.992), exceeding the frozen LLM-only baseline evaluated on the same set (macro--score 0.493, exact match accuracy 0.621,±1-class accuracy 0.981). On the validation set used for architecture selection, the ensemble outperformed structured-only ML (XGBoost macro--score=0.333, <.001), and the LLM-only model reached a macro--score of 0.642 (95% CI 0.525‐0.691), nominally exceeding the expert panel ceiling. Per-class analysis attributed this to a perfect score on the 2 validation ASA-PS 5 cases. Excluding that class, the adjusted macro--score was approximately 0.55, within the range of the parallel ensemble. The LLM component also generated explanations detailing comorbidities, severity descriptors, and functional status indicators. Conclusions: The parallel ML-LLM ensemble achieved performance approaching the theoretical ceiling established by the expert panel benchmark while providing interpretable clinical explanations. The ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968‐0.992) may enhance operational safety by minimizing extreme misclassifications. This approach demonstrates how complementary AI architectures can enhance perioperative risk assessment, which is particularly valuable given current health care workforce shortages.
title: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification: Hybrid Machine Learning–Large Language Model Ensemble Retrospective Validation Study

summary: Background: Advances in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer have substantially improved survival, resulting in a growing population of survivors of childhood cancer who may experience long-term treatment-related sequelae. Cognitive late effects are an important long-term consequence of childhood cancer and can affect cognitive functioning, psychosocial well-being, and quality of life. Digital health interventions offer accessible and flexible approaches to managing cognitive difficulties among children with cancer. However, the existing evidence has not yet been comprehensively synthesized. Objective: This study aimed to map and synthesize the existing evidence on digital health interventions for cognitive management among children with cancer; characterize intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components; and identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research. Methods: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Six academic databases, including PubMed, Embase (Ovid), CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically searched for relevant studies published between January 2010 and August 2026. Eligibility criteria were developed using the population-concept-context framework. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Screening was performed independently at the title/abstract and full-text stages, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were used to synthesize the findings. Results: A total of 5371 records were identified through the literature search. Following screening, 19 publications representing 14 independent study samples and involving 566 children with cancer were included. Four digital health modalities were identified: computer-based interventions, internet-based interventions, mobile apps, and neurofeedback training. Computer-based interventions were the predominant modality. Across these modalities, working memory and attention were the most frequently targeted cognitive domains, while feasibility, acceptability, and adherence were the most commonly assessed implementation-related outcomes. However, relatively few interventions incorporated coach support, telephone-based communication, or educational components, and none evaluated economic outcomes. Conclusions: Although digital health interventions show promise for supporting cognitive function in children with cancer, substantial gaps remain in the current evidence. This scoping review mapped the field according to intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components, rather than focusing solely on the efficacy of individual technologies. Future research should prioritize the development of multidimensional, personalized, and functionally integrated digital health interventions that combine cognitive training with supportive care, education, monitoring, and communication. Multicenter randomized controlled trials should subsequently evaluate these interventions using clinically meaningful outcomes, with comprehensive assessments of safety, adherence, implementation, and health economic outcomes to establish their effectiveness, feasibility, and sustainability.
title: Application of Digital Health Interventions for Cognitive Management in Children With Cancer: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) show great potential for widespread application in the field of nursing; however, their limitations include hallucinations, insufficient domain knowledge, and delays in updating evidence. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), by combining external knowledge retrieval with text generation, holds promise for optimizing model outputs. However, current evidence on the use of RAG in nursing remains fragmented and has not been systematically synthesized. Objective: This scoping review aims to map the applications of RAG in the nursing field, identify current research characteristics and gaps, and provide a foundational evidence base to inform future research and development of intelligent tools for nursing practice. Methods: This study adopted the Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and followed PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting standards. We systematically searched 9 databases—PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Scopus, CNKI, VIP Database, Wanfang Database, and Sinomed—from inception to September 2026. Backward and forward citation searches were also conducted to identify additional eligible studies. Eligible publications were restricted to those in English or Chinese during study selection. Two independent reviewers completed study screening and data extraction, and descriptive synthesis was performed for all eligible records. Results: A total of 28 studies published between 2024 and 2026 were included. The application of RAG in nursing primarily focused on 4 scenarios: patient education (n=9), nursing informatics (n=8), clinical decision support (n=7), and nursing education (n=4). The base LLMs included the GPT series, LLaMA, ChatGLM, and Doubao, among others, while the knowledge bases primarily integrated literature, clinical guidelines, institutional resources, and clinical data. Most studies relied on dense retrieval, while some incorporated hybrid retrieval, knowledge graphs, and reranking to achieve optimization. Generation and task-output evaluations were reported in 27 studies, whereas retrieval evaluation, safety and reliability evaluations, and implementation or outcome evaluations were less frequently reported. Only 4 studies were conducted in real-world clinical settings. Overall, RAG demonstrated potential to improve the accuracy and reliability of LLM-generated outputs in specific nursing tasks; however, most studies validated only in simulated environments. Conclusions: This review systematically maps and synthesizes the application scenarios, technical characteristics, reporting completeness, evaluation methods, and research outcomes of RAG from the perspective of nursing tasks, further refining the evidence landscape for RAG research in nursing contexts. By summarizing the selection of base LLMs, knowledge bases and retrieval processes, the key elements of technical reports, and the areas for tiered evaluation, this review provides evidence-informed considerations for the design, validation, and reporting of future RAG-based nursing AI systems. The findings may assist clinical nurses, nursing educators, and hospital IT teams in identifying application scenarios, key safety requirements, and evaluation priorities, while also highlighting the necessity of conducting prospective validation within real-world nursing workflows.
title: Applications, Technical Characteristics, and Evaluation Approaches of Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Nursing: Scoping Review

summary: Safe deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography (NCCT) demands high sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) across common and uncommon findings requiring clinical attention. Here, we present a collaborative safety net integrating BrainCT-CLIP, a generalist foundation model via contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), with commercial detectors. Every examination remained in the reporting workflow, deprioritized only when no model returned a positive result. In a retrospective multicenter external validation of consecutive emergency and trauma cohorts (n = 2001), standalone commercial detectors left 31 of 324 remarkable examinations deprioritized, including 16 target-disease false negatives and 15 outside their indications. In contrast, the collaborative system recovered every remarkable examination at a threshold prespecified in the development cohort, achieving 100% sensitivity and NPV while deprioritizing 18% of examinations (368/2001; 95% CI, 17–20). These findings support generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization under radiologist oversight, with high sensitivity for intracranial findings requiring clinical attention.
title: Collaborative generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography

summary: Background: Mobility recovery after critical illness is a complex and multidimensional process. Digital health technologies have emerged as approaches for delivering rehabilitation, monitoring recovery, and facilitating self-management among intensive care unit (ICU) survivors. However, the extent to which current digital health approaches address the multidimensional nature of mobility recovery remains unclear. Objective: This scoping review aimed to map the current evidence on digital health approaches supporting mobility recovery among ICU survivors and to examine the mobility domains, outcomes, feasibility, and acceptability associated with these approaches. Methods: A scoping review was conducted following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and was reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from January 2016 to September 21, 2026. Studies involving adult ICU survivors that used digital health approaches to assess, monitor, support, or promote mobility recovery were included. Mobility outcomes were mapped to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health domains of body functions and structures, activities, and participation. Clinical outcomes were synthesized separately from implementation and user experience outcomes. Results: Twenty-seven reports representing 24 unique parent studies were included. Digital health approaches comprised telemedicine, telerehabilitation, mobile health, wearable monitoring, virtual reality, robot-assisted rehabilitation, and digital recovery platforms. Telemedicine and telerehabilitation were the most frequently reported approaches, and exercise-based rehabilitation was the predominant intervention component. Mobility outcomes were heterogeneous and concentrated on body functions and structures and activity-level performance, particularly muscle strength, exercise capacity, and functional performance, whereas participation outcomes were less frequently represented. Controlled and comparative studies showed mixed between-group findings, with clinical benefits not consistently demonstrated across primary or mobility-related outcomes. In contrast, feasibility, adherence, usability, and acceptability were generally favorable when assessed, although technical difficulties and incomplete device-generated data were reported in some studies. Conclusions: Digital health technologies offer diverse approaches to supporting mobility recovery after critical illness, but current evidence remains concentrated on physical function and activity-level outcomes, with limited attention to participation and long-term recovery. More rigorous and longitudinal studies using standardized, multidimensional mobility outcomes are needed to clarify clinical effectiveness and support sustainable implementation.
title: Digital Health Technologies for Mobility Recovery Among Intensive Care Unit Survivors: Scoping Review

summary: Digital health may extend cardiovascular care in communities with limited specialist access, but its effectiveness depends on whether communities have the infrastructure, devices, affordability, and capacity needed to use digital services. We linked national data on cardiometabolic disease burden, cardiology workforce, and digital readiness across 82,999 US census tracts. Among high-burden tracts in counties with no cardiologist or declining per-capita cardiologist supply, 4,765 (18.0%) tracts representing 19.9 million residents had higher digital readiness and were thus classified as deployment-priority tracts, whereas 21,752 (82.0%) tracts representing 74.1 million residents had lower readiness and were investment-priority tracts. Investment-priority tracts were spread across the urban-rural continuum and faced different barriers (adoption versus infrastructure). Contrasting classifications frequently occurred among neighboring census tracts within the same metropolitan area, highlighting geographic variation not captured by county-level targeting. Findings were broadly consistent across nine additional analyses with varying measures of readiness, workforce access, and classification thresholds. These findings provide a national framework for distinguishing communities where digital cardiovascular care may be deployed from those where infrastructure and adoption support may first be needed to enable equitable implementation. As presented at 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions: Analysis of U.S. Census and other national health data identifies communities with high cardiovascular care needs and assess health system readiness for digital care deployment.
title: Digital readiness for cardiovascular care in high-burden US communities with cardiology workforce constraints

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Clinical communication skills are a core yet complex competency in medical education and practice. However, early-stage medical students often struggle to apply communication frameworks in practice due to limited opportunities for structured simulation training. Generative AI (GenAI)–supported training has the potential to offer a scalable and innovative approach for clinical communication skills training. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study examined the longitudinal development of medical students’ clinical communication skills over 1 academic year and investigated whether AI-powered simulation contributed to differential improvement relative to conventional training. In addition, the study explored motivational, behavioral, and affective mechanisms associated with communication skills development. <strong>Methods:</strong> A nonblinded randomized controlled design was used at a medical school in the United Kingdom, with students assigned either to the control group (n=28, 56%) or to the AI group (n=22, 44%), who practiced with SimPatient, a patient-simulator chatbot accessed through a web browser. Communication skills performance was assessed using standardized objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) scores relative to the pass marks to enable comparison across time points. Paired <i>t</i> tests and difference-in-differences (DID) analyses were conducted between groups and over time to examine changes in communication skills. Latent change score modeling was used to identify predictors of communication skills change. Sentiment analysis was conducted on 6120 comments from AI-student conversations. Finally, a system quality survey was used to assess participants’ feedback on the AI-powered simulator. <strong>Results:</strong> Latent change score modeling showed that gains in intrinsic motivation and behavioral learning were significant predictors of students’ communication skills change. The AI group showed a greater descriptive increase in communication skills than the control group, yet the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Within the AI group, consultations whose lexical tone trended more strongly toward resolution (consultation tone) were descriptively associated with communication skills improvement; given the small subsample (n=17), this finding is reported as exploratory. The AI group’s confidence level in AI use was negatively associated with communication skills improvement, while the group nevertheless reported a generally high level of satisfaction with the system. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> In this study, medical students’ clinical communication skills increased over the academic year, with this development most strongly associated with their motivation and behavioral engagement; the AI-supported group did not differ significantly from conventional training. The simulator responded appropriately and provided a usable environment for practicing foundational communication behaviors but was limited in capturing the affective complexity, vulnerability, and narrative unpredictability of real clinical encounters. In conclusion, this study suggests that GenAI holds promise for supporting foundational clinical communication training and providing positive practice environments, thereby fostering motivation and behavioral engagement.
title: Evaluating an AI-Powered Patient Simulator for Communication Skills Training: One-Year Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Frontline health workers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often face barriers that compromise care quality, including limited training, high patient loads, inadequate access to updated clinical guidance, and resource constraints. Working in underserved settings further exacerbates challenges to providing accurate, complete, and empathetic responses. Addressing these gaps requires innovative tools to support FLWs in real time. Objective: This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ChatGPT-3.5 (OpenAI) in enhancing the quality of FLWs’ responses to health inquiries in Lagos, Nigeria. Methods: In this observational study, 36 licensed frontline health workers (doctors, nurses, and community health workers) practicing general or primary care in Lagos, Nigeria, generated responses to 15 patient-generated health questions covering maternal and neonatal health, family planning, and sexually transmitted infections. Each FLW produced responses using their own knowledge and available resources (human-only) and with ChatGPT-3.5 assistance (GPT-aided). A panel of 4 clinicians evaluated responses using a 5-point Likert scale for accuracy, empathy, contextualization, completeness, safety, and overall preference. In addition, 8 nonclinician health seekers assessed a subset of responses across 3 themes: Caring, Trust, and Ease of Understanding. Results: Across 1080 responses from 36 frontline health workers, GPT-aided responses significantly outperformed human-only responses on all clinician-rated metrics (<.001), with the largest gains observed in completeness, empathy, and overall preference, particularly among community health extension workers (CHEWs). Nonclinician evaluators also favored GPT-aided responses across all themes, with a strong preference for trust. Conclusions: This study provides empirical evidence that a large language model (ChatGPT-3.5) enhances the completeness, empathy, and perceived trust of responses by frontline health workers in Lagos, Nigeria. These findings underscore the potential of integrating ChatGPT-3.5 to strengthen health care delivery in resource-limited settings, highlighting the necessity for capacity building and further investigation into its safe, equitable, and effective implementation.
title: Evaluating Frontline Health Workers’ Responses to Patient Inquiries With and Without Large Language Model Support in Nigeria: Observational Study

summary: Background: The integration of AI-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (AI-CDSS) into clinical practice has expanded rapidly, particularly in medical imaging. Beyond algorithmic performance, growing evidence suggests that clinicians’ engagement with AI-CDSS is shaped by how transparently systems communicate their outputs, and how trust is formed through human-AI interaction. However, a limited understanding of how these concepts are perceived by end users and developers continues to hinder real-world implementation. Objective: This study aims to explore expert perspectives on transparency and trust in AI-CDSS for chest X-ray diagnosis, with a focus on the two-dimensional lens: user interface and users’ mental models. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semistructured interviews with a total of 21 experts, including 11 radiologists and 10 AI experts experienced in AI-CDSS. Data were analyzed thematically to explore factors perceived to influence transparent communication and trust. Results: Three themes emerged: (1) perspective of transparency and trust, (2) user interface, and (3) users’ mental models. Findings reveal that trust is a dynamic calibration process developed through repeated use, feedback loops, and alignment with clinicians’ mental models, rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. Significant discrepancies were identified between how developers design system transparency and how clinicians interpret AI outputs. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that transparency and trust are achieved through interpretable outputs, clear communication of system limitations, and alignment with clinical workflows. Designing trustworthy AI-CDSS requires integrating transparent interface design with consideration of users’ knowledge, experience, and attitudes to support effective human-AI interaction.
title: Expert Perspectives on Transparency and Trust in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis: Qualitative Study

summary: Online medicine sales have not only improved access but also expose consumers to illegal online medicine vendors (IOMVs) selling substandard/falsified products. This study provides the first pan-European assessment of exposure to legitimate online pharmacies (LOPs) and IOMVs in search engine results (SERs). We scraped the top-50 Google results in 30 European countries for six tracer active pharmaceutical ingredients across three categories: controlled substances, prescription-only medicines (POMs), and over-the-counter products (OTCs). Links were categorised as LOPs or IOMVs based on official registries. From 9000 SERs, 3839 linked to medicine-selling websites (63.7% LOPs, 36.3% IOMVs). LOPs outnumbered and outranked IOMVs, though IOMV:LOP ratios reached 2.37 (Norway) and 2.18 (Cyprus). Search engine redirection affected 56.6% of IOMV links. IOMV prevalence increased with regulatory control: 1.4% (paracetamol), 5.5% (ibuprofen), 10.2% (omeprazole), 55.1% (amoxicillin), 76.2% (alprazolam) and 77.5% (clonazepam). IOMV links were less likely to be highest-ranked and less common in the top-10 SERs in countries permitting online OTC and POM sales, than in those prohibiting them. Despite LOP dominance, Europeans face substantial exposure to IOMV links, higher for controlled substances and in countries prohibiting online sales. Harmonised regulatory action, supported by search engine providers, is needed for safer online medication access.
title: Exposure to legitimate and illegal online medicine vendors via search engines in 30 European countries

summary: Pregnancy dating fails the women who need it most: those who reach care without a first-trimester scan. We externally validated a commercial image-only ultrasound deep-learning model for delivery-date prediction, applied unmodified to 64,235 frames from 3788 examinations of 2550 pregnancies (34% migrant) at four Chilean public hospitals. Mean absolute error was 6.9 days versus 11.6 for the conventional due date, yet most of this gain reflected a shorter local gestation and fell below one day against recentred comparators. Fixed-term comparators assign every pregnancy the same gestational age at birth and therefore cannot rank who will deliver early, at any level of point accuracy: accuracy metrics are blind to the ranking on which management turns whenever the outcome distribution is concentrated, as in term-dominated cohorts. In a prespecified landmark analysis the model’s separate image-only risk score discriminated preterm birth with an area under the curve of 0.86, against 0.52 for gestational age alone; outside the landmark restriction it exceeded a clinical baseline of coded diagnoses plus same-examination biometry by 0.09, although it was miscalibrated. Error and calibration were also assessed by maternal nationality. These classification analyses are exploratory, and no woman was managed with the model; they identify what a prospective study should test.
title: External validation of an image-only ultrasound model for delivery-date prediction in four Chilean public hospitals

summary: Background: Smartphone-based self-assessment methods, such as ecological momentary assessment (EMA), are increasingly used to measure perceived stress in research and emerging clinical applications. However, the proliferation of studies and methods has made it difficult for researchers and practitioners to maintain an overview and make informed methodological choices. An updated synthesis of smartphone-based self-report methods is therefore needed. Objective: This scoping review aims to systematically map smartphone-based methods for assessing self-reported perceived stress in healthy adults during daily life, to describe measurement characteristics and methodological choices, and to narratively examine the extent to which validity and reliability evidence are reported. Methods: Following PRISMA‑ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines, we searched a total of 7 databases: Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM, and PsycInfo. Eligible studies assessed general perceived stress in healthy adults using smartphone-based self-report measures in daily life. Screening was conducted independently by at least 2 reviewers at the abstract and full‑text levels. Methodological characteristics of stress measurement were extracted and summarized descriptively. Results: From 8777 deduplicated records, 108 studies met all eligibility criteria. Publication frequency increased notably over the review period. Most studies used observational designs, with EMA-style prompting schedules. Stress was typically assessed using very brief measures: most instruments (84/114, 74%) consisted of a single item, most commonly answered using a Likert-type scale or a visual analog scale. Measurement frequency ranged from once per week to multiple prompts per day, with intensive approaches (≥3 prompts per day) being most common. Despite the prevalence of these instruments, only a minority of studies reported validity or reliability measures. When provided, evidence typically consisted of correlations with established stress questionnaires or affective measures. A small subset conducted elaborate psychometric analyses or validation of instruments. Conclusions: Smartphone-based stress assessment is widespread but methodologically heterogeneous. This review provides an updated methodological overview to support researchers in selecting or developing robust smartphone-based measures of perceived stress. Only a small minority of studies reported formal psychometric evaluations, highlighting the need for more systematic validation of smartphone-based stress assessment. Trial Registration: OSF Registries 7UM6B; https://osf.io/7um6b
title: Measuring Perceived Stress in Healthy Adults in Daily Life: Scoping Review of Smartphone-Based Self-Assessment

summary: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P) Overview On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued the Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) proposed rule. This rule proposes regulatory revisions to the Conditions of Participation (CoPs), Conditions for Coverage (CfCs), and Requirements for Participation for Medicare- and Medicaid-participating providers and suppliers (collectively referred to as CoPs). These revisions would reduce costs, increase transparency, enhance flexibility for providers to deliver innovative patient care, and streamline existing regulations. It also proposes to rescind certain Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers. Background CMS conducted a comprehensive review of the CoPs for all 21 provider and supplier types, as well as some payment policies, to identify opportunities to reduce administrative burden while maintaining patient safety and quality care. The agency identified obsolete, outdated, and excessively burdensome regulations that CMS proposes to eliminate or reform to enhance the effectiveness of facility operations and reduce unnecessary burden or other costs, with a particular focus on freeing up resources that healthcare providers could otherwise use to improve patient health and safety. Collectively, CMS estimates the proposals would save $320 million, returning more than 3.26 million hours of staff time to providers. This proposed rule would alleviate unnecessary regulatory burden through deregulation in the following ways: Hospitals Remove the staff training requirements for transfer protocols and emergency services readiness (both currently effective), and obstetric (OB) care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by hospitals that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons. Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) Remove the staff training requirements related to emergency services readiness (currently effective) and OB care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by CAHs that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons. Revise regulations to clarify current CMS policy that CAH distance eligibility determinations are based on proximity to hospitals that provide acute care inpatient services or another CAH. Implement new statutory requirements to allow CAHs that meet certain qualifying criteria, as defined by the statute, to be exempt from the distance eligibility requirements. Long-Term Care (LTC) Facilities Remove the COVID-19 vaccine requirements related to educating staff about the benefits and risks, offering the vaccine, and documenting these actions. Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for residents. Remove the continuing respiratory illness data reporting requirement while retaining the requirement for specific reporting during a future Secretary-declared public health emergency (PHE). Modify the requirement for LTC facilities to provide a state ombudsman with notice of resident transfers related to emergent care. Revise the requirements for the active involvement of representatives of direct care staff in conducting the LTC facility assessment. Revise the physical environment requirements to exempt existing facilities from the room occupancy and bathroom facility standards. Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICFs/IID) Remove the requirements related to educating staff about the COVID-19 vaccine and its benefits and risks, offering it to them, and documenting these actions. Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for clients. Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs) Remove expired COVID-19 and seasonal influenza reporting requirements related to ongoing data reporting and staff vaccination. Remove REH data reporting requirements during a PHE. Physical Environment Life Safety Code (LSC) and Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) Updates and Emergency and Standby Powers Systems (ESPS) Codes Adopt the 2024 editions of National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) LSC and HCFC and the 2022 edition of the ESPS Codes. Outside Window or Door Requirement Remove the requirement that patient care areas have access to natural light and ventilation through exterior windows and doors for hospitals, CAHs, and other providers with similar regulations (Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institutions, LTC facilities, ICFs/IID and hospice inpatient care facilities). Waiver Authority Codify in the regulations CMS’ authority to permit facilities to comply with specific provisions of a newer edition of the LSC or HCFC. Medicaid Payment Transparency for Nursing Facilities and ICFs/IID Rescind the following Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers: The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for direct care workers, The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for support staff, and The percentage of Medicaid payments for ICFs/IID services spent on compensation for support staff. Comment Solicitations CMS is including comment solicitations in this proposed rule to obtain input from interested parties related to the following topics: Allowing LTC facility residents to opt-out of having a discharge notice sent to the state ombudsman office; Strategies to minimize burden for hospitals and CAHs to comply with ongoing respiratory illness and PHE infectious illness data reporting requirements; Approaches to allow flexibility for providers regarding the requirement for physician supervision of certified registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs); Expanding the scope of practice of physician assistants and nurse practitioners providing care in LTC facilities, especially as it pertains to performing visits currently required by a physician; Revising criteria for transplant program initial certification to reduce barriers to entry for new transplant programs while maintaining patient safety and ensuring the transplant program’s competence; and Future policies to address Medicaid institutional workforce shortages and strengthen the institutional workforce. View the final rule on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-22812/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-cutting-administrative-requirements-for-excellence-in-patient-care . CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P)

summary: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Final Rule (CMS-4215-F) On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that codifies policies established in guidance documents for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (“Negotiation Program”) for initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond (CMS-4215-F). For initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028 of the Negotiation Program, statute directed CMS to implement the Negotiation Program through program instruction and other forms of program guidance. With this authority expiring, CMS is codifying the Negotiation Program for 2029 and beyond. In addition to codifying these policies, we are establishing new policies to continue implementation of statutory provisions under the Negotiation Program as well as finalizing revisions or clarifications to certain policies previously established to incorporate lessons learned from ongoing experience. 1 The Negotiation Program final rule is one of several activities that reflect a broader CMS-wide strategy to lower prescription drug costs for people with Medicare. CMS is approaching codification of the Negotiation Program consistent with the goals of achieving greater value for beneficiaries and taxpayers and continuing to foster innovation. The final rule is effective Dec. 5, 2026. Background on the Negotiation Program Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (P.L. 117-169) establish the Negotiation Program to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. Specifically, in accordance with section 1191(c)(3) of the Social Security Act (the Act), MFP means, with respect to a year during a price applicability period and with respect to a selected drug (as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to such period, the MFP negotiated in accordance with section 1194 of the Act, and updated to account for inflation in accordance with section 1195(b) of the Act, as applicable, for such drug and year. Under the IRA, with respect to each initial price applicability year, CMS will: (1) publish a list of selected drugs for negotiation and renegotiation, if any; (2) enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs that choose to participate; (3) negotiate (or renegotiate) MFPs for such selected drugs; (4) publish any agreed-upon MFPs for selected drugs; (5) carry out administrative and compliance duties; and (6) impose civil monetary penalties (CMPs), when applicable. CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Part D and/or payable under Part B for initial price applicability year 2029 and for each subsequent initial price applicability year. In addition to the drugs selected for negotiation, CMS may also select drugs for renegotiation if selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP meet certain eligibility and selection criteria. Codification of the Negotiation Program In codifying the requirements for the Negotiation Program, CMS builds upon policies established for the first three cycles of negotiations and establishes new requirements for the fourth and future cycles of negotiations with a particular focus on continuing to increase transparency in the Negotiation Program. The final regulations include, but are not limited to: Identification of Selected Drugs. Section 1192 of the Act establishes the requirements governing the publication of the selected drug list for an initial price applicability year, the identification of selected drugs, ranking of negotiation-eligible drugs, and the identification of qualifying single source drugs. CMS codifies these policies consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, with a new policy to clarify how CMS will identify qualifying single source drugs to address potential program integrity concerns posed by specific new formulations. Additionally, CMS clarifies the treatment of withdrawn approvals for indications when identifying whether a drug that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion meets eligibility criteria to be a qualifying single source drug, in accordance with amendments made by the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation (Pub. L. 119-21). Requirements for Manufacturers of Selected Drugs. Section 1193(a) of the Act establishes the Negotiation Program Agreement and the requirements for a willing primary manufacturer to enter into and sign the Negotiation Program Agreement no later than Feb. 28 following the selected drug publication date. The Negotiation Program Agreement will remain in effect, including through renegotiation, as applicable, until the selected drug is no longer considered a selected drug under section 1192(c) of the Act (due to a determination that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing) unless it is terminated sooner by the primary manufacturer under specified conditions. CMS finalizes additional details related to the primary manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to another entity. In addition, CMS codifies the timing and process for executing and terminating a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS and the requirements a willing primary manufacturer is subject to upon executing the Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS, including mandatory submission of data to CMS, consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Negotiation Factors. After entering into an Agreement with CMS and in accordance with section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, the primary manufacturer of each selected drug must submit the following information with respect to the selected drug: information on the non-Federal Average Manufacturer Price (non-FAMP) and any information that CMS requires to carry out the Negotiation Program, including but not limited to, information related to the manufacturer-specific factors listed in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act. Additionally, primary manufacturers and any interested party may voluntarily submit evidence about the selected drugs and potential therapeutic alternatives as described in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. In accordance with section 1194(e) of the Act, CMS uses manufacturer-specific data and available evidence about the selected drugs and their therapeutic alternatives as the basis for determining offers and considering counteroffers in the negotiation process. CMS codifies these policies, including submission requirements for primary manufacturers, requirements for primary manufacturers to update submitted data, and how CMS will consider evidence from comparative effectiveness studies. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Negotiation Process. CMS develops and uses a consistent methodology and process for negotiation with the aim of achieving agreement on “the lowest [MFP] for each selected drug” in accordance with section 1194(b)(1) of the Act. The negotiation process includes engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, including patients; the development and delivery of the written initial offer, including a concise justification, to the primary manufacturer of a selected drug; the ability for the primary manufacturer to accept an offer or provide a statutory written counteroffer; optional negotiation meetings between CMS and the primary manufacturer; additional price exchange opportunities; the conclusion of negotiation, including a final offer sent by CMS to the primary manufacturer, where applicable; and the publication of agreed-upon MFPs and explanations of such MFPs. CMS codifies these policies for the negotiation process, including engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, the offer and counteroffer process, and the publication and explanation of the MFP. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Ineligibility for Selection, or Deselection of a Selected Drug Before or During Negotiation, or Following the Negotiation Period . In accordance with sections 1192(c) and 1192(e) of the Act, a potential qualifying single source drug is not eligible for selection, a selected drug will no longer be subject to the negotiation process, and a selected drug will cease to be a selected drug, subject to certain timing and situations, if CMS determines: (1) the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a generic drug under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that identifies as its reference-listed drug a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable), or FDA has licensed a biosimilar under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act that identifies as its reference product a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable); and (2) the generic drug or biosimilar, as applicable, is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure. CMS codifies provisions regarding its identification of when such generic drug or biosimilar is marketed within the meaning of these statutory requirements (“Bona Fide Marketing”). Further, CMS codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to the determination of ineligibility of a potential qualifying single source drug that would otherwise be eligible for selection and to the determination of the deselection of a selected drug, with additional information provided on the points in time CMS reviews the information to determine if a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. CMS also codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to monitoring that the approved generic drug(s) or licensed biosimilar(s) continue to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing for any potential qualifying single source drug(s) that were previously considered ineligible for selection or for any selected drug(s) deselected because CMS determined that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. These policies are consistent with statute and build on CMS guidance regarding the timing of review of the information to evaluate whether a generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. Renegotiation of an MFP. Section 1194(f) of the Act establishes the requirements governing the identification of renegotiation-eligible drugs, the selection of drugs for renegotiation, and the renegotiation process. CMS codifies the criteria CMS will use to determine renegotiation eligibility and selection, the types of information CMS will consider when determining renegotiation eligibility and selection, opportunities and requirements for data submission, and the process for renegotiation, which will remain consistent, to the extent practicable, with the process and methodology used for negotiation. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. For renegotiation with respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond, CMS finalizes its policy to consider the agreed-upon MFP for a drug selected for renegotiation as part of the consideration of section 1194(e)(1) factors. Strengthening Program Integrity to Address Fixed Combination Drug Loophole Under policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, if a drug is a fixed combination drug with two or more active moieties, active ingredients, or, for a vaccine for infectious disease(s), antigen components, a potential qualifying single source drug is identified using the same distinct combination of active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components. Under this policy, CMS is aware of a program integrity risk
title: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Final Rule (CMS-4215-F)

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who achieve clinical pregnancy following fresh in vitro fertilization (IVF)/intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) carry an elevated miscarriage risk. However, individualized risk stratification after clinical pregnancy confirmation but before outcome determination remains challenging in clinical practice. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop, externally and prospectively validate over time, and interpret a machine learning–based risk stratification model for women with PCOS who had achieved a confirmed clinical pregnancy after fresh IVF/ICSI. <strong>Methods:</strong> This multicenter study included 8911 clinical pregnancy IVF/ICSI cycles across development (n=7241; miscarriages: n=973), external validation (n=1170; miscarriages: n=146), and prospective temporal validation (n=500; miscarriages: n=62) cohorts. Prespecified predictors contained no observed missing values; training-fold median imputation was kept only as a leakage-safe fallback. A total of 13 candidate machine learning and traditional statistical algorithms were compared internally using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (5 repeats) within the development cohort; preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning were performed exclusively in training folds. A prelocked Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model was carried forward unchanged for external and prospective temporal validation. Cross-fitted logistic recalibration of averaged XGBoost out-of-fold probabilities was evaluated as a secondary development-sample diagnostic analysis. Model performance encompassed discrimination, precision-recall, calibration, threshold-based metrics, decision curve analysis, risk stratification, and Shapley additive explanations–based interpretability. <strong>Results:</strong> Miscarriage rates were 13.4% (973/7241), 12.5% (146/1170), and 12.4% (62/500) for the development, external validation, and prospective temporal validation cohorts, respectively. In repeated cross-validation, XGBoost (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.885, 95% CI 0.874-0.896) and LightGBM (AUC 0.882, 95% CI 0.871-0.893) showed comparable discrimination; the paired XGBoost-LightGBM DeLong test was not significant (Holm-adjusted <i>P</i>=.07). Raw XGBoost out-of-fold probabilities overestimated absolute risk (mean predicted risk 30.3% vs observed risk 13.4%); cross-fitted recalibration within the development cohort improved calibration but was not propagated to validation cohorts. The locked XGBoost model achieved AUCs of 0.787 (95% CI 0.748-0.827; Brier score 0.099) in external validation and 0.763 (95% CI 0.709-0.816; Brier score 0.104) in prospective temporal validation, showing cross-cohort performance attenuation. Risk-quartile stratification using fixed development-cohort cutoffs showed consistent event enrichment across validation cohorts, but positive predictive values remained modest. Shapley additive explanations analysis identified anti-Müllerian hormone, endometrial thickness on the day of human chorionic gonadotropin administration, and basal luteinizing hormone as leading predictors. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> The locked XGBoost model using routine preoutcome variables may support miscarriage risk stratification and counseling for women with PCOS with clinical pregnancy after fresh IVF/ICSI. Given cross-cohort discrimination loss and calibration drift, it should serve only as a risk-ranking tool, not for diagnosis or treatment selection. Local calibration monitoring is mandatory before any real-world clinical deployment.
title: Miscarriage Risk Prediction for Women With Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Who Achieve Clinical Pregnancy After Fresh Embryo Transfer: Multicenter Development, Geographic External Validation, and Prospective Temporal Validation Study

summary: Analyses disentangling the role of the gut microbiome in linking lifestyle factors to health outcomes remain limited. Here, using fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort, we identified two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. A health-associated axis enriched in microbial metabolism of dietary components was linked to plant-based, soy and dairy intake. In contrast, a disease-associated axis, enriched in oral-derived bacteria and pathobionts, was linked to refined carbohydrates and sedentary behavior. Starter culture microorganisms used to ferment foods did not show statistically significant mediation of the observed health effects. Alcohol was associated with both health- and disease-oriented mediation patterns involving microbial host-glycan utilization. Microbiome-defined health- and disease-oriented mediator axes were supported by fecal short-chain fatty acids and plasma cytokines from >1,700 individuals, revealing butyrate-associated anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory host profiles, respectively. Microbiome-based prediction (MADE) scores captured lifestyle–microbiome–disease mediation patterns and distinguished individual diseases across 13 independent external cohorts from the United States, China, Sweden, Russia and Australia. We identify the gut microbiome as a key mediator linking lifestyle to health and disease, providing a framework for microbiome-based assessment to guide lifestyle interventions for health promotion and disease prevention. Fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort and microbiome-based prediction scores validated across 13 independent and geographically diverse cohorts revealed two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases.
title: Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases

summary: Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. Here we developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, which was recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults. Our purpose was to capture the full pattern of a person’s movement and use it to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems. Gait is conventionally described by engineered features (for example, calculated measurements such as cadence and stride length), which may fail to capture the fine detail of how a person moves. Our model instead translates movement into learned embeddings: sets of numbers that describe how all body joints move together over time. Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearsonʼs r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area (r = 0.83), and embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline model using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use. Anatomical ablation analyses revealed that leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. These findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal, motivating integration of gait analysis into routine clinical assessment as a scalable, passive vital sign. A gait foundation model, developed using three-dimensional skeletal motion data from 3,328 adults, predicts a wide array of clinical characteristics and diagnoses, including cardiometabolic, mental health and frailty phenotypes.
title: A gait foundation model for prediction of multisystem health phenotypes from 3D skeletal motion

summary: Affordable electroencephalography (EEG) headsets could widen access to EEG-based treatment and assessment, but require rigorous validation. We evaluated PainWaive, a custom-developed 2-channel central scalp EEG headset designed for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain. Eighty participants completed two resting-state EEGs using PainWaive and a research-grade system (LiveAmp). Alpha, beta and theta power, and peak alpha frequency (PAF), were derived from homologous central channels. PainWaive demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.72–0.93), with beta and theta ranging from moderate-good (ICCs = 0.42–0.76). Across 160 home-based neurofeedback sessions in two chronic pain samples, reliability was good-to-excellent across metrics (ICCs = 0.72–0.88). Spectral-shape correlations between PainWaive and LiveAmp were excellent (r > 0.91). Cross-device agreement was moderate-to-good for alpha power and PAF (ICCs = 0.53–0.74), but weaker for beta and theta (ICCs = 0.16–0.51). Sensitivity analyses showed alpha power and PAF were robust across choices, whereas beta and theta agreement varied by pipeline. Overall, PainWaive demonstrated reliable measurement of central scalp EEG metrics, supporting repeated within-device monitoring. Cross-device findings showed correspondence with research-grade EEG for some measures but should not be interpreted as establishing direct numerical interchangeability between systems. These findings provide a technical foundation for future remote EEG and neurofeedback studies in chronic pain.
title: Evaluation of PainWaive: a consumer-grade EEG headset for remote EEG monitoring and neurofeedback research in chronic pain
